title: Death’s Decree Runs Through All Creation
intro: Abu al-Hasan al-Tihami mourns a son who died as a child in Ramla. Al-Bakharzi, who copied the elegy in his youth, calls the boy Abu al-Fadl. The father begins as though consoling anyone who has lost someone, until the child comes into view as a star at daybreak and a crescent that never grew full. A grave within whispering distance and the father’s sleepless nights give way to a vision of the men who would have defended the boy if death could be resisted. Later the father looks at what grief and time have made of his own body and temper.

translation: Death’s decree runs through all creation.
This world is no abiding home.
1.sharh: He speaks as though a verdict has already been delivered. It covers everyone, although the particular death that moved him to speak has yet to be named.

translation: One moment a man is seen telling the news,
the next he is news himself.
2.sharh: The onlookers remain while the man's part changes. In the time it takes to pass from one half-line to the next, the teller has become the thing told.

translation: The world was fashioned turbid, yet you would have it
clear of every mote and trace of mud.
3.sharh: The demand for a clear draught is directed at a world made cloudy from the outset. A mote can spoil both water and the eye through which one judges its clarity.

translation: To demand of the days the opposite of their nature
is to look for a live ember in water.
4.sharh: The impossibility is physical. Water would put out the very ember sought in it, just as the conditions of living undo the demand for a life without grief.

translation: Whenever you hope for the impossible,
you build your hope on a crumbling brink.
5.sharh: Hope takes on the weight of a building. Its foundation is the edge already giving way, an image familiar from the crumbling bank in Qur'an 9:109.

translation: Life is sleep and death an awakening.
Between them a man is a passing night-vision.
6.sharh: A dream figure is seen without being held. Calling death the awakening makes the apparently solid person in the interval as elusive as a visitor in a dream.

translation: Whether the soul accepts this or refuses,
it follows where the reins of destiny lead.
7.sharh: The soul can consent or protest. Neither response puts the reins into its own hands, a distinction between attitude and destination that matters to a grieving father.

translation: Attend to your needs in haste.
Your lives are journeys among journeys.
8.sharh: He turns to his listeners in the plural. A traveller has business to finish before moving on, and no traveller owns the road or the time left on it.

translation: Race on the horses of youth. Make haste
before they are reclaimed. They are on loan.
9.sharh: Youth offers more than time. It supplies the very mounts by which one goes fast, and ownership of those mounts belongs to someone who can call them in.

translation: Time beguiles you with promises. It chokes you even as
it gives you pleasure, and lays waste to what it built.
10.sharh: Time can make even the mouthful it gives stick in the throat. The same agent acts as builder and destroyer, so its first kindness gives no assurance of the next.

translation: However hard you try, time will not make peace.
Hostility to the freeborn is its nature.
11.sharh: He treats Time as an adversary with whom terms might have been sought. Its hostility to people of independent spirit prepares for the personal complaint that now breaks through.

translation: I have been bereft of a keen, bright blade
that I laid by to avenge old wrongs.
12.sharh: The son is first named by what the father hoped he would become. Bereaved of a future defender, he finds himself the injured man for whom that defender was being kept.

translation: I praise him in his wake. Had he
been spared envy, I would have praised him for his deeds.
13.sharh: The father can praise his son now only in his wake, though he had hoped to praise deeds that others could see. The word for envy could also evoke fear of the evil eye. An early variant says outright that the boy was taken before his time.

translation: Star, how brief your life was,
as brief as the lives of stars before dawn.
14.sharh: A star first noticed before dawn has only a little time left to shine for its watcher. Its apparent lifespan gives the father a measure for his son's.

translation: Crescent of a few days, you passed before you rounded
into a full moon, before your waning time came.
15.sharh: The boy missed both the full moon of maturity and the darkness that would ordinarily close its cycle. The father returns to this crescent in another elegy for Abu al-Fadl. There he says he hoped to see it grow full, only for fate to overtake it at the very start of the month.

translation: Eclipse overtook you before its time
and erased you before the full moon was due.
16.sharh: The eclipse comes to a crescent still waiting to grow full. The disturbance of lunar time registers what death has done to the order the father expected.

translation: He was drawn out from his playmates and age-mates
like an eyeball drawn from its lids.
17.sharh: His companions still form a ring around a place he once occupied. The repeated verb makes their loss as intimate and irreplaceable as an eye pulled from between its lids.

translation: It is as though my heart were his grave,
and he a secret folded deep inside it.
18.sharh: The heart becomes a second burial place, accessible only to its owner. A secret remains fully present to the person who keeps it even while everyone else is shut out.

translation: If he draws envy though so young, many a person of consequence
looks small in the eyes of those who gaze.
19.sharh: The printed and recited word raises the possibility of envy even at so young an age. Another old reading turns the question toward the spectator who underestimates a slight figure.

translation: The stars, for all the height of their station,
look small. Small they are not.
20.sharh: Distance accounts for the deceptive scale. The father has already called the boy a star, so this observation about size also defends a life cut short before the world could measure it.

translation: A child is part of the man you come to console.
When part of a man goes, the whole follows.
21.sharh: A visitor offering condolences may imagine two separate people, one dead and one intact. The father represents his own remaining life as footsteps following the child's.

translation: I weep for him, then say, by way of apology,
“Fortunate you, to have left the meanest of homes.”
22.sharh: His tears might sound like a wish to bring the boy back. The apology admits that leaving this world may have been fortunate from the child's side of the parting.

translation: I live beside my enemies. He lives beside his Lord.
How far apart our two neighbourhoods are.
23.sharh: In the language of protection, living beside someone also means being under that person's care. The father asks himself which of the two has the better neighbour.

translation: I complain of your distance, yet where you lie
you could hear me whisper, were it not for death.
24.sharh: He chooses a whisper to establish just how close the grave is. No ordinary distance could make a conversation at such close range impossible.

translation: East lies closer to west
than those five handspans are to me.
25.sharh: He could measure the earth between them with his own hand. Turning five handspans into a greater distance than the width of the world measures separation in another sense.

translation: Too late. The snares of death have caught you.
The reaper of lives has stolen your years.
26.sharh: “Too late” interrupts the wish that a whisper might still arrive. The boy is caught in one image and deprived of his years in another, without an act of his own.

translation: You and I ran toward the same finish.
You have reached it. Your father is still on the track.
27.sharh: The unexpected event is the finishing order. The child started later and reached the end first, while the father still has the length of the course ahead.

translation: Whenever I speak, you are the first thing I say.
Whenever I fall silent, you are in my thoughts.
28.sharh: The two halves leave no time unaccounted for. To an outsider his voice comes and goes, but silence simply changes the child's place from speech to inward thought.

translation: I conceal the fire of my anguish
as firesticks conceal the fire they can kindle.
29.sharh: A firestick can look cold before it is struck. Outward composure is compatible with the continued presence of everything needed for a blaze.

translation: I press my sighs down as they rise
and keep wiping away the tears as they flow.
30.sharh: He gives the sighs their own upward motion, which he must physically resist. The doubled sounds of the wiping verb suggest a hand returning again and again to the eyes.

translation: The flame of grief burns brighter if I yield to it.
If I resist, it goes into hiding.
31.sharh: The alternative to burning openly is burning out of sight. The sound of the Arabic verb for kindling returns inside the word for hiding, as though the fire remained in it.

translation: I hold the fires of sorrow in. Often, though,
grief overcomes my patience and showers sparks.
32.sharh: Forbearance is a sustained effort here. Sparks are the small, visible escapes that betray the larger fire when the effort momentarily fails.

translation: The garment of pretence shows what lies beneath.
Wrap yourself in it and you stand bare.
33.sharh: The remark about pretence grows directly out of his attempts to hide grief. A transparent wrap becomes most revealing at the moment its wearer relies on it for cover.

translation: Have my lids grown short, or the gap between them wide?
Was my eye fashioned without lashes?
34.sharh: He runs through imaginary defects in the eye's construction. Sleeplessness feels anatomical, as if the two lids had never been made to meet.

translation: My eyes shun sleep. Even a brief doze
pricks like a sword edge when I close them.
35.sharh: The same word, ghirār, names both a snatch of sleep and a blade's edge. The very instant at which relief should come becomes the point of pain.

translation: Should my lids invite a spell of sleep,
the current between them would sweep it away.
36.sharh: The lids would be hospitable to sleep if they could. Tears become a current strong enough to wash the invited guest away.

translation: I keep the long nights alive as they put me to death.
The first clear light of dawn puts them to death.
37.sharh: “Giving life” to a night is an idiom for staying awake through it. Taken literally, the idiom sets up a chain of deaths, the speaker's at night and the night's at daybreak.

translation: Until I see dawn, its hand coming to know
by touch of light the flap of a pitch-black tent.
38.sharh: Night is a pitch-black tent. In this reading the hand of dawn feels its way about the flap with light. Al-Bakharzi has a more explicit motion, a hand lifting the curtain.

translation: Dawn has flooded the stars, like
a torrent rising and flowing over blossoms.
39.sharh: Dawn is now a flood instead of a hand. The stars disappear as scattered blossoms do when a sheet of water passes over them, still there but lost to the observer.

translation: Had you been someone arms could protect, young men of ours
would have waded for you through seas of spearheads and blades.
40.sharh: The long description of the clan opens under an impossible condition. Their courage could have saved the boy from any foe their weapons could actually reach.

translation: They would have spread a second earth of blood above the earth,
then built a sky of dust.
41.sharh: Blood lies just above the ground and hoof dust hangs overhead. Between them the imagined rescue would have manufactured both a floor and a sky.

translation: When these men put on their armour, you would take it
for clouds buttoned over moons.
42.sharh: The faces shine like moons. Buttons or fastenings make the cloudy armour something that even a moon could put on, joining a celestial image to the act of dressing.

translation: Look at the swords of the mail-clad men.
They are channels thrust out by the hands of seas.
43.sharh: The men themselves are seas and the swords running out of their hands are narrow inlets. Metal has acquired the first of several appearances of water.

translation: If they levelled their right arms, so long are they,
they could thrust with them in place of the quivering spears.
44.sharh: To have a long reach can suggest bounty as well as physical power. Here the arms alone would do the work of the flexible lances the riders carry.

translation: Proud-eyed men. When battle fails them, they go seeking it
from every quarter, as men go seeking rain.
45.sharh: Pastoral travellers followed reports of rain to grazing land. The fighters' eagerness gives the search for battle the energy of a community searching for the next rainfall.

translation: They led their chargers beside the riding camels
and alternated there between saddles and camel seats.
46.sharh: The two kinds of saddle record the changes of mount. Leading the horses alongside the camels lets the men travel without spending all their horses' strength at once.

translation: As though they had filled their armour bags
and the ribs of their blades with a desert mirage.
47.sharh: The eye goes from the bags that hold the mail to the gleaming line down each blade. Both seem awash with the shimmer a traveller might mistake for water. In al-Bakharzi’s reading, “scabbards”, the sword too is seen through its container.

translation: As if the maker of the long coats of mail were deceived
by the steel’s watery lustre and fashioned still water
48.sharh: Arabic can call a blade's sheen its “water.” The armourer is imagined taking the expression literally and trying to work a pool of standing water. The object he fashions comes in the next verse.

translation: into chain links, securing each meeting of a ring
with a bubble in the place of a rivet.
49.sharh: The watery illusion survives close inspection. Even the small rivet that closes each link looks like a bubble fixed to the surface.

translation: They clothed themselves in sheets of frozen water
and veiled their faces with bubbles of running water.
50.sharh: The body of the coat has the solidity of ice. Around the head, where the links fall and move, the same metal looks like bubbles travelling on a stream.

translation: Lions, yet they give others precedence over their own provisions.
Lions do not live by such generosity.
51.sharh: The lion has carried the comparison as far as courage. The moment food is set down, the animal ceases to be an adequate measure of the men.

translation: Their handsome faces adorn the gathering
as moons adorn their haloes.
52.sharh: The meeting-place becomes a halo that owes its beauty to the body within it. The moon-faces earlier seen inside armour now light a gathering at peace.

translation: They lavish their treasures on the neighbour in their midst
with the tenderness of foster mothers.
53.sharh: The old word includes foster mothers and animals that nurse another's young. It explains how a stranger admitted to the clan can receive the tenderness of kinship.

translation: Each man has made sword edges his allies.
So nobly have they served that he needs no other help.
54.sharh: The grammatical subject of “proved noble” is the sword edges. They earn the title of allies by giving the fighter the support normally expected from other men.

translation: When he cradles his lance under his arm, you would think it
a viper tucked beneath a ravening lion’s foreleg.
55.sharh: The long bending lance supplies the snake and the warrior supplies the lion. Tucking a thing under the arm is a precise physical pose beneath the extravagant double image.

translation: Yet a lion, if you spring at it, can rely
only on its fangs and claws.
56.sharh: The lion comparison is tested a second time, now for its equipment. The animal enters every encounter with the same limited set of weapons.

translation: The rings of fine mail under the thrusts of his lance,
in the press of a great host packed tight.
57.sharh: The compact text leaves the rings hanging without a stated comparison. A longer recension likens them to bracelets on an archer's wrist, then carries the lance into the packed ranks. The recording joins the two surviving halves.

translation: Between soil drenched in blood and slippery underfoot
and dust stirred up by the mounted chase.
58.sharh: The same soil behaves in two ways. Where it is wet a foot might slip, while the dry ground rises into the air under the pursuing horses.

translation: Humiliation lies hidden in the shade of taking it easy.
Great rank is won by taking great risks.
59.sharh: Kindred sounds connect ease with abasement. The second half turns on the old sense of “weight or rank” in a word that also evokes the danger one incurs to obtain it.

translation: His brow and his right hand grow moist
both in hardship and in ease.
60.sharh: Moisture can literally stand on the brow, and dew on a hand is a familiar image for gifts. His manner and his giving survive the change in his means.

translation: Toward every generous deed he stretches fingers
with channels for livelihood running between them.
61.sharh: The gaps between the fingers turn into waterways. The plenty that travelled figuratively through the warriors' swords now reaches dependants through an open hand.

translation: He wins distinction by earning it or prevailing.
In its cause he is courted, and he courts others.
62.sharh: The warrior has to negotiate as well as prevail. Reading the first verb as passive gives him two roles, the man whose goodwill others seek and the man who must approach them tactfully. The on-screen text instead has him draw close to others.

translation: Stars have appeared in the night of my youth.
Give them time and they will turn to daylight.
63.sharh: At first the white hairs are separate points in black hair. Their promise of daybreak is the promise of eventually covering the whole head.

translation: The burning of my insides has whitened my parting.
This light is the flame of that fire.
64.sharh: The whiteness visible to a stranger is traced to an invisible internal fire. Loss has reached the surface of the body despite the effort to conceal it.

translation: The hair at my nape is grey. On every bough
the lush dark foliage turns at last to blossom.
65.sharh: The greying reaches the back of his head. Looking at a bough in bloom allows him to regard the change of colour as one stage in a natural sequence.

translation: Like draws like. Why, then, do the fair beauties
shy away from the white in his parting?
66.sharh: Women likened to pale statues ought, by his playful rule of resemblance, to be attracted to white. The same colour that conventionally enhances a face marks age in the hair.

translation: They would gladly take the black centres of their hearts
and the black of their eyes to dye my temples.
67.sharh: They could supply a dye only by surrendering something of themselves. The pupil is visibly black, while the “black of the heart” is its innermost core.

translation: Let the gazelles not shy from him. They have seen
how plants change from season to season.
68.sharh: Calling the women gazelles gives them grounds for knowing better. An animal living on pasture has witnessed many changes of colour in the plants on which it feeds.

translation: Two things dissolve at the first touch,
the shade of youth and a bad man's friendship.
69.sharh: Shade can disappear before the person sheltering under it has moved. So can a friendship that seemed perfectly real until the first demand was made on it.

translation: No welcome to faithful grey hair. Welcome
to the shade of youth, that treacherous betrayer.
70.sharh: The moral adjectives describe the duration of a visit. Grey hair faithfully stays and youth deserts him, yet the guest he wants back is the fickle one.

translation: What I wanted from the world was youth and its first bloom.
When it passed, my wishes passed with it.
71.sharh: The first bloom of youth was the condition for everything else he wanted. The one desire in the first half becomes all his desires in the second.

translation: Short was the distance it travelled.
Its kindnesses and gifts were never small to me.
72.sharh: He can measure how briefly youth stayed without measuring its value by that brevity. The same idea of shortness fits its tenure and fails to fit its gifts.

translation: The richer we grow, the heavier our worries.
Utter poverty lies in accumulating more.
73.sharh: Accumulation creates the next object of need. A person who possesses more but always needs more has lost the very independence wealth was supposed to buy.

translation: Anything beyond a traveller's provisions is left behind,
lost to accident, an heir, or some new mischance.
74.sharh: The provisions recall the journey near the opening. Excess can pass to an heir even in the best ordinary course of events, without being of any use to the man who saved it.

translation: I pity those who envy me for the heat
of the rancour they harbour in their breasts.
75.sharh: Pity is an unexpected response to envy. He regards the heat within his opponents' own bodies as punishment already under way.

translation: They look at what God has done for me. Their eyes
are in a garden, their hearts in a fire.
76.sharh: The same sight gives two organs radically different surroundings. It costs the eyes nothing to enjoy the garden that the heart experiences as fire.

translation: I bear no blame. I tried to hide my merits,
as though I had veiled the face of my daylight.
77.sharh: The apology contains a boast. To say that his merits cannot be hidden assigns them the visibility of daylight even as he protests his modesty.

translation: I covered them with modesty. They craned
their necks above the curtains.
78.sharh: He gives his excellences necks of their own. They can defeat their owner's attempt at concealment by the ordinary act of peering over a curtain.

translation: Some men are landmarks, others uncharted ground.
Among the stars are dim ones and brilliantly clear ones.
79.sharh: A landmark does more than stand out. Other people can find their way by it. Unequal visibility among the stars adds a second measure of human distinction.

translation: Men look alike when they bring their herds to water.
They show their different worth when they bring them away.
80.sharh: Anyone can arrive at the watering place with a herd. Bringing it away after the animals have actually drunk provides the test, as results distinguish people who began alike.

translation: By my life, I made the roads to eminence easy for them.
Blind to them, they could not follow my tracks.
81.sharh: He claims to have walked the road on their behalf as well as pointed it out. His tracks should give those who come after him all the guidance they need.

translation: Had they looked with their hearts, they would have understood.
Blindness of insight is a blindness of the eyes.
82.sharh: To see tracks and to recognise a way forward are different acts. The repeated root for sight ties that failure of understanding to the apparent blindness of his followers.

translation: Why did they not strive as generous men do and succeed,
or accept the places allotted by fate?
83.sharh: The envious might try for the distinction themselves or come to terms with their share. Continuing to watch another man's good fortune leaves them stuck in the condition already described.

translation: Nobility and fidelity have gone from humankind.
They linger only in poems.
84.sharh: A poem can keep the names of virtues in circulation after people have ceased to practise them. This very line gives the lost qualities somewhere to live.

translation: Betrayals have spread among trusted men and everyone else,
until we even doubt what our eyes see.
85.sharh: Betrayal by a trusted witness does the gravest damage. Once confidence in testimony collapses, suspicion reaches even the evidence of one's own eyes.

translation: Sometimes a prudent man needs a fool's support.
A right hand is little good without a left.
86.sharh: The comparison is functional. Even the culturally favoured right hand is limited on its own, as a wise man may be when circumstances demand another person's help.

translation: Bless the blows of misfortune. They are
rust to the base, a polisher to the free.
87.sharh: The same ordeal tarnishes one piece of metal and polishes another. The shift back to shining steel prepares for the father's account of what hardship has made of him.

translation: What was I but a lump of iron? They forged me
into a sword and their changes set my edge free.
88.sharh: Misfortunes now do the forging. Early on he mourned the son he had stored up like a blade. Here it is the survivor whose edge the years have brought out.

translation: An age like a mother dog, tender toward her pup
and turning away from the fierce lion’s cub.
89.sharh: The age recognises its own pup and has no care for a lion's young. After so much praise of lions and their courage, the final figure is again a cub that greatness cannot protect.

1.1.2.head: المَنِيَّة
1.1.2.meaning: Death as the fate allotted to a living thing.

1.1.4.head: البَرِيَّة
1.1.4.meaning: Created beings, the population over which death holds sway.

2.1.1.meaning: While or just as, introducing a state about to change abruptly.

3.2.3.head: الأَقذاء
3.2.3.meaning: Motes or bits of debris in an eye or a drink.

4.2.4.head: جَذوَة
4.2.4.meaning: A glowing brand or live ember. Classical sources allow three initial vowels.

5.2.4-5.head: شَفير هار
5.2.4-5.meaning: A bank or brink that is giving way under its own weight.

6.2.3-4.head: خَيال سارٍ
6.2.3-4.meaning: A night visitor or vision that passes through a dream.

7.2.2.head: زِمام
7.2.2.meaning: A rein or leading cord. The verse puts the reins in destiny’s hands.

8.1.2.head: مَأرَب
8.1.2.meaning: A need or purpose one sets out to fulfil.

8.2.2.head: سَفَر
8.2.2.meaning: A journey. The vowel on the f distinguishes it from sifr, a book.

9.2.4.head: عارِيَّة
9.2.4.meaning: A thing lent for use and due to be returned to its owner.

10.1.4.head: أَغَصَّ
10.1.4.meaning: To make someone choke on what he receives.

11.2.1.head: خُلُق
11.2.1.meaning: A habitual disposition, here attributed to time.

12.1.2.head: وَتَرَ
12.1.2.meaning: To bereave someone or leave him with a blood claim. The verse uses the passive.

12.1.3.head: صارِم
12.1.3.meaning: A keen-edged sword, here the son on whom he counted.

12.2.2-3.head: طِلابَة الأَوتار
12.2.2-3.meaning: The pursuit of blood claims, redress for the killing of kin.

13.1.3.head: إِثر
13.1.3.meaning: In his wake, after he has passed on. This sounds close to the word for lasting works.

13.2.2.head: اِغتُبِطَ
13.2.2.meaning: To be regarded with envy. With the undotted Arabic letter ع, the verb instead means to be taken while still young.

14.2.4.head: سَحَر
14.2.4.meaning: The last part of the night, immediately before dawn.

15.2.5.head: سِرار
15.2.5.meaning: The dark end of the lunar month when the moon disappears.

16.2.3.head: مَظِنَّة
16.2.3.meaning: The occasion or point at which something may be expected.

16.2.4.head: الإِبدار
16.2.4.meaning: The moon’s coming to the full.

17.1.3-4.head: أَتراب وَلِدات
17.1.3-4.meaning: Age-mates and children born about the same time.

17.2.4.head: شُفر
17.2.4.meaning: The rim of an eyelid where the lashes grow, or the lashes themselves.

19.1.2.head: اِغتُبِطَ
19.1.2.meaning: To be envied. Another reading makes him “be thought little of” because of his size.

21.1.2.meaning: The bereaved person to whom condolences are offered.

21.2.5.head: الأَثَر
21.2.5.meaning: A track left for another. Here the survivor follows the deceased.

22.2.4.head: أَلأَم
22.2.4.meaning: Meanest or most ignoble, said of this world.

23.2.1.meaning: An exclamation marking a great difference or separation.

24.2.5.head: سِرار
24.2.5.meaning: Whispered or confidential speech. Earlier the same form named the dark of the moon.

25.1.5.head: شُقَّة
25.1.5.meaning: A stretch of distance, especially one difficult to traverse.

25.2.5.head: شِبر
25.2.5.meaning: A handspan, measured from the tip of the thumb to the little finger.

26.1.4.head: شَرَك
26.1.4.meaning: A snare or trap, here set by death.

27.2.4.head: المِضمار
27.2.4.meaning: A ground for training horses, hence a racecourse.

28.2.5.head: إِضمار
28.2.5.meaning: Holding a thought inwardly without speaking it.

29.2.4-5.head: الزِّناد الواري
29.2.4-5.meaning: A firestick or striker capable of giving fire.

30.2.1.head: كَفكَفَ
30.2.1.meaning: To check repeatedly or wipe away again and again.

30.2.2.head: عَبرَة
30.2.2.meaning: A falling tear. The plural means the tears he keeps trying to hold back.

31.2.1.meaning: To give or kindle fire, set against the following concealment.

32.2.2.head: التَّصَبُّر
32.2.2.meaning: The effort of making oneself endure.

33.1.3.head: شَفَّ
33.1.3.meaning: To be thin enough to show what lies underneath.

35.2.5.head: غِرار
35.2.5.meaning: The cutting edge of a blade, a different sense of the word for a nap.

36.1.2.head: اِستَزارَ
36.1.2.meaning: To invite someone to visit, here a welcome offered to sleep.

37.1.2-3.head: لَيالي التَّمّ
37.1.2-3.meaning: Long nights that run their full length, especially in winter.

37.2.2.head: تَبَلُّج
37.2.2.meaning: The first clear breaking of light through the dark.

38.1.4.head: أَلِفَ
38.1.4.meaning: To become familiar with something. Al-Bakharzi's reading has dawn lifting the flap.

38.2.2.head: رَفرَف
38.2.2.meaning: A hanging flap or curtain of a tent.

38.2.4.head: القار
38.2.4.meaning: Pitch, used as a measure of blackness.

39.2.5.head: النُّوّار
39.2.5.meaning: Blossoms, the points covered by the imagined flood.

40.2.3.head: عامِل
40.2.3.meaning: The forepart of a spear adjoining its head, hence the spears themselves.

41.1.1.head: دَحا
41.1.1.meaning: To spread or lay out over a surface.

42.2.2.head: مُزَرَّر
42.2.2.meaning: Fastened or buttoned, as though the cloud were clothing.

43.2.1.head: خَليج
43.2.1.meaning: A channel or inlet running out from a larger body of water.

44.2.4-5.head: القَنا الخَطّار
44.2.4-5.meaning: The long lances that sway or quiver as they are carried.

45.1.1.head: أَشوَس
45.1.1.meaning: Proud or dauntless men, their sidelong gaze a sign of bearing.

45.1.5.head: اِنتَجَعَ
45.1.5.meaning: To seek fresh pasture. Here the men seek the place of battle.

46.1.1.head: جَنَّبَ
46.1.1.meaning: To lead a spare mount alongside the animal being ridden.

46.2.4.head: كور
46.2.4.meaning: A riding saddle for a camel, as distinct from a horse’s saddle.

47.1.3.head: عَيبَة
47.1.3.meaning: A bag or chest for equipment, here for storing armour.

47.2.1.head: عَمود
47.2.1.meaning: The ridge running down the middle of a blade. Al-Bakharzi gives ghumud, the scabbards that hold the blades.

47.2.2.head: نَصل
47.2.2.meaning: A blade, especially the metal of a sword.

48.1.4.head: سابِغَة
48.1.4.meaning: A long, ample coat of mail.

48.2.1-2.head: ماء الحَديد
48.2.1-2.meaning: The sheen or water of polished steel.

49.2.1.head: حَبابَة
49.2.1.meaning: One bubble on the surface of water.

50.1.1.head: تَسَربَلَ
50.1.1.meaning: To put on a garment around the body.

51.1.3.head: آثَرَ
51.1.3.meaning: To give someone else preference, here in sharing provisions.

52.1.2.meaning: A gathering place or the people assembled there.

53.2.1.head: مُنفِسَة
53.2.1.meaning: A possession prized enough that an owner would be reluctant to part with it.

53.2.3.head: ظِئر
53.2.3.meaning: A foster mother or an animal induced to nurse another's young.

54.1.5.head: ظُبَة
54.1.5.meaning: The cutting edge or point of a sword.

55.1.3.meaning: To hold a lance close, tucked under the arm.

56.1.3.head: ثاوَرَ
56.1.3.meaning: To spring upon or grapple with an opponent.

57.1.2.head: الدِّلاص
57.1.2.meaning: Smooth, finely made coats of mail. A longer reading compares their rings to bracelets.

57.2.4.head: الجَرّار
57.2.4.meaning: Vast and slowly drawing its great numbers along.

58.2.2.head: نَقع
58.2.2.meaning: Dust raised by the hoofs of moving horses.

59.1.4.meaning: Ease, going gently, or taking things at leisure.

59.2.4.head: الإِخطار
59.2.4.meaning: Incurring danger or putting something valuable at risk.

60.1.2.head: أَسِرَّة
60.1.2.meaning: Lines or creases of the face, especially the brow.

61.2.3.head: أَثناء
61.2.3.meaning: The spaces or folds between things, here the fingers.

62.2.2.head: دارى
62.2.2.meaning: Read here as a passive, to be approached tactfully. The diwan and the on-screen text have an n in the verb, giving the sense of drawing near.

63.2.5.head: الإِسفار
63.2.5.meaning: Daybreak as the light spreads and becomes clear.

65.1.2.head: القَذال
65.1.2.meaning: The back of the head, above the nape.

65.2.1-2.head: فَينان أَحوى
65.2.1-2.meaning: Abundant branching growth, so deep a green that it looks dark.

66.1.4-5.head: بيض الدُّمى
66.1.4-5.meaning: Fair women likened to graceful sculpted figures.

67.2.4.head: عِذار
67.2.4.meaning: The hair along the side of the face.

68.1.3.head: ظَبيَة
68.1.3.meaning: A gazelle, conventionally a figure for a beautiful woman.

71.1.1.head: وَطَر
71.1.1.meaning: A desire one longs to fulfil.

71.1.5.head: رَوق
71.1.5.meaning: The first bloom and choicest part of youth.

74.2.6.head: عارٍ
74.2.6.meaning: A visitation or unforeseen mischance that overtakes someone.

75.2.4.head: وَغر
75.2.4.meaning: Rancour that burns inwardly. The word also suggests heat.

77.2.2.head: بَرقَعَ
77.2.2.meaning: To cover a face with a veil.

79.2.4.head: دُرِّيّ
79.2.4.meaning: A brilliant star. The verse sets such stars beside faint ones.

80.1.4.head: إيراد
80.1.4.meaning: Bringing animals to a watering place.

80.2.4.head: الإِصدار
80.2.4.meaning: Bringing a herd back from water after it has drunk.

81.1.3.head: أَوطَأَ
81.1.3.meaning: To make a path easy to tread.

84.2.1.head: تَصَرَّمَ
84.2.1.meaning: To come to an end. The dual verb refers to generosity and fidelity together.

86.1.2.meaning: To seek another’s support, literally to take him as a supporting arm.

87.1.1-2.head: لِلَّهِ دَرُّهُ
87.1.1-2.meaning: An idiom of admiration, unexpectedly addressed to misfortunes.

87.2.3.head: صَيقَل
87.2.3.meaning: A polisher of blades, or a polishing tool.

88.1.4.head: زُبرَة
88.1.4.meaning: A lump of iron before it is worked.

88.1.5.head: طَبَعَ
88.1.5.meaning: To fashion or forge metal into a blade. The acting subject is the misfortunes.

88.2.4.head: غِرار
88.2.4.meaning: A sharpened edge, now the speaker’s own. Earlier it pricked his sleepless eyes.

89.1.4.head: رَئِمَ
89.1.4.meaning: To show instinctive tenderness and attachment to one's young.
